title: Spot the Mate
subtitle: Six hidden mates-in-one from real attacking patterns.
goals: Recognize six classic mating pictures instantly
Build the pattern library every attack draws on

steps.say: Strong players don't calculate mates — they RECOGNIZE them. This speed round shows six classic mating pictures, each one move away. No hints needed if the pattern is in your head; that's the goal. Ready?

steps.prompt: Mate in one — the ARABIAN mate. Knight and rook, corner king.
hints: The f6 knight already covers g8 — and it can protect a rook that comes very close.
Capture on h7: the rook is untouchable under the knight's guard.

line.say: The Arabian mate — the oldest recorded mating pattern, from medieval shatranj manuscripts. Knight guards rook, rook guards everything else.

steps.wrongSay: The knight on f6 guards both g8 AND h7. Which rook move uses that?
steps.successSay: Knight on f6 (or f3, c6, c3) + rook to the corner file: burn the shape in.

steps.prompt: Mate in one — the pawn wedge on g6 is the whole story.
hints: The g6 pawn controls h7 — so a queen landing there is protected.
Take the h7 pawn. The king has nowhere left.

line.say: Damiano's picture: a humble pawn on g6 turns h7 into a supported mating square. Whole attacking systems exist just to plant that pawn.

steps.wrongSay: Which square does your g6 pawn defend? Put the queen there.
steps.successSay: Pawn on g6 = queen mates on h7. One of the most common winning patterns in club chess.

steps.prompt: Mate in one — the queen-and-bishop battery fires down the long diagonal.
hints: Your queen and bishop both aim at h7 along b1–h7. Count the defenders of h7: zero.
The queen lands on h7 with the bishop backing her up.

line.say: The battery mate: queen touches the king, bishop guards the queen from across the board. The ...h6 pawn push never saves anyone from this.

steps.wrongSay: Queen and bishop share the b1–h7 diagonal. Where do they strike together?
steps.successSay: Batteries mate at a distance — the defender never sees the far-away bishop doing the real work.

steps.prompt: Mate in one — but the back rank looks defended...
hints: The d8 rook guards the back rank — but who guards the ROOK?
Capture d8. Your queen supports from f3... no wait — check what really protects the capture: nothing needs to! Count the escape squares.

line.say: The 'defended' back rank had one guard and you attacked it once — with mate. The f7/g7/h7 wall did the rest. Guards that are merely equal in number always lose the back rank.

steps.wrongSay: The back-rank guard hangs. Take it — and count why the recapture never comes.
steps.successSay: A guarded back rank falls when the guard itself is attacked. Always count one level deeper.

steps.prompt: Mate in one — the king's own rooks are his pallbearers.
hints: The rooks on c8 and e8 block their own king's escape — the 'epaulettes' on his shoulders.
Strike straight down the file, one knight's-breath away from the king.

line.say: The epaulette mate! The queen covers c7, d7 and e7 from d6, and the king's own rooks seal the back rank. Crowded kings die in their own furniture.

steps.wrongSay: The king can't use c8 or e8 — his own rooks live there. Cover everything else with one queen move.
steps.successSay: When pieces crowd their king, every check gets deadlier. The epaulette is the family photo of that idea.

steps.prompt: Last one — mate in one, knight and rook conspiring.
hints: Your f5 knight covers g7 and h6 — the dark escape squares.
The e8 rook is the only back-rank guard, and your rook attacks it.

line.say: Back rank plus knight net: g7 was covered by the f5 knight, so capturing the guard ended everything at once. Two patterns stacked — that's how real mates happen.

steps.wrongSay: Combine two ideas: the knight seals the dark squares, the rook deals with the guard.
steps.successSay: Six patterns, six kills. When these pictures live in your head, you'll find them in YOUR games — often when your opponent thought they were defended.
